subject: Career
title: The Regret Minimization Framework
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: The Regret Minimization Framework.

hook.text: Jeff Bezos asked: 'At 80, will I regret not trying this?' He quit finance to start Amazon.

buildup.text: The regret minimization framework: project yourself to old age and look back at your choices.

discovery.text: Bronnie Ware's research on the dying found the #1 regret: 'I wish I'd had the courage to live true to myself.'

twist.text: People rarely regret things they tried, even if they failed. They regret the paths they never took.

climax.text: When deciding on a transition, ask: 'Which choice will I regret NOT making in 20 years?'

punchline.text: Minimize future regret. That's the compass.

quiz.question: What was the #1 regret of the dying according to Bronnie Ware's research?
options: Not having the courage to live true to themselves

details.summary: Jeff Bezos popularized this decision-making tool: project yourself to age eighty and ask which choice you would regret less. It cuts through short-term fear by reframing decisions on a lifetime horizon.
details.whyItMatters: Fear of failure dominates short-term thinking, but regret over inaction compounds over decades. This framework shifts the calculus toward bold, values-aligned decisions.
takeaways: Imagine yourself at eighty evaluating today's decision
Regrets of inaction typically outweigh regrets of action
The framework is most useful for irreversible life decisions

faq.question: Does the regret minimization framework work for smaller career decisions?
faq.answer: It is most powerful for major crossroads like changing industries or starting a business. For smaller decisions like choosing between two similar roles, other tools like weighted pro-con lists provide more practical granularity.

faq.question: What if you genuinely cannot predict which choice you would regret more?
faq.answer: When both paths seem equally regrettable or promising, default to the option that maximizes learning. More learning opens more future doors, which reduces the probability of long-term regret regardless of the outcome.
